en: (Now begins the first chapter) [The Section on the Four Ancillaries] 1.1.1: From the knowledge of the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), tenet (*siddhānta*), members of a syllogism (*avayava*), reasoning (*tarka*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), discussion (*vāda*), contentious debate (*jalpa*), destructive cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

{Padārthoddeśasūtra} 1.1.2: Upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the removal of each preceding one, resulting in liberation (apavarga).
{Padārthoddeśasūtra}
[The Section on the Means of Valid Cognition] 1.1.3: Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition.
(The Sūtra Enumerating the Means of Valid Cognition)
1.1.4: Perception is the knowledge arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbal, unerring, and of a determinate nature. (This is the definition of perception.
1.1.5: Now, inference, which is preceded by that [perception], is of three kinds: pūrvavat, śeṣavat, and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa.

The definition of inference (1.1.5): [Inference is] the knowledge of an object through its connection with a well-known mark. The definition of comparison (1.1.6): Comparison is the means of establishing what is to be established through similarity to something well-known.
1.1.7: Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person; this is the definition of verbal testimony.
1.1.8: It is of two kinds, because its objects are either perceived or unperceived.

{The distinction of terms} [Section on the Objects of Cognition] 1.1.9: The objects of cognition (prameya), however, are the self, body, sense organs, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation.
{The Sūtra on the Enumeration of Objects of Cognition} 1.1.10: Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self; this is the definition of the self.
1.1.11: The body is the substratum of movement, the sense organs, and their objects; [this is the definition of the body].
1.1.12: The olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, and auditory organs are the sense organs derived from the elements.
1.1.13: {The definition of the sense-faculties}:
Earth, water, fire, air, and space are the primary elements {the definition of the elements}.

1.1.14: Odor, taste, color, touch, and sound are the qualities of earth and the other elements; these are the objects [of the senses] (the definition of an object being that which is the domain of the senses).
1.1.15: Intellection, apprehension, and knowledge are synonymous.
1.1.16: The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind (*manas*). This is the definition of the mind.
1.1.17: Activity (pravṛtti) is the initiation of speech, thought, and body; this is the definition of activity. 1.1.18: The defects (doṣas) are characterized by incitement to action.
Rebirth after death is the definition of *pretyabhāva* (the state after passing away).
1.1.20: An object produced by activity and defects is the result; this is the definition of a result.
1.1.21: Suffering is characterized by affliction.
1.1.22: Liberation (*apavarga*) is the absolute release from that [suffering];
this is the definition of liberation (*apavargalakṣaṇa*).
[The Section on the Definition of the Preliminary Limb of Reasoning] 1.1.23:

Doubt is a deliberation requiring further investigation, arising from the perception of common or multiple properties, from conflicting testimony, and from the lack of a settled determination regarding perception or non-perception. (This is the definition of doubt.)

1.1.24: That object for the sake of which one proceeds is the purpose (*prayojana*). [This is the definition of purpose. 1.1.25: That object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among both common people and investigators is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

{The Definition of an Example} [The Section on the Definition of the Tenets Based on Logic] 1.1.26: A tenet (*siddhānta*) is the established position resulting from the acceptance of a system (*tantra*), a topic (*adhikaraṇa*), or a personal admission (*abhyupagama*).

1.1.27: The definition of the tenet established by admission (*abhyupagamasiddhānta*): It is fourfold, because of the difference in its status as a tenet for all schools, a tenet for a specific school, a tenet concerning a particular context, and a tenet accepted for the sake of argument; this is the aphorism enumerating the divisions of the treatise (*tantra*).
1.1.28: A tenet established in a treatise that is not contradicted by any other treatises is a *sarvatantrasiddhānta* (tenet accepted by all schools).

[This is the definition of a *sarvatantrasiddhānta*. 1.1.29: A tenet established in one's own school but not established in other schools is a *pratitantrasiddhānta* (tenet specific to a particular school).
1.1.30: *Pratitantrasiddhānta-lakṣaṇam*: That, upon the establishment of which there is the establishment of another topic, is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.
*Adhikaraṇasiddhānta-lakṣaṇam*: The definition of a topical conclusion.

1.1.31: The postulate of a doctrine is the examination of the specific details of that which has been accepted without prior critical investigation; this is the definition of the postulate of a doctrine (*abhyupagamasiddhānta*).
[Nyāya Treatise]
1.1.32: The thesis, reason, example, application, and conclusion are the members [of a syllogism]. (This is the sūtra enumerating the members.
1.1.33: The statement of that which is to be proven is the thesis.
{The definition of the thesis} 1.1.34: The reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) through its similarity to the example (*udāharaṇa*).
{The definition of the reason}
1.1.35: Likewise, the definition of a reason (*hetu*) is by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
1.1.36: An example (*udāharaṇa*) is an instance that possesses the property of the probandum (*sādhya*) due to its similarity to it.
1.1.37: The definition of the example (udāharaṇa) is the opposite of that [definition of the thesis], or else it is the reverse.
1.1.38: The application (*upanaya*) is the connection of the subject (*sādhya*) with the example, either as "so it is" (*tathā*) or "not so it is" (*na tathā*). 1.1.39:
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the presentation of the reason (*hetu*).

[The Section on the Subsequent Members of the Syllogism] 1.1.40: Hypothetical reasoning (*tarka*) is the deliberation for the sake of knowing the true nature of an object whose true nature is not yet known, based on the occurrence of a logical ground.
{The definition of deliberation (tarka)} 1.1.41: Determination of the truth after having deliberated by means of the thesis and the counter-thesis is ascertainment (nirṇaya).
{The definition of ascertainment}
(Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Adhyāya in the Nyāyasūtra.
(Now begins the second Āhnika: The Section on the Definition of Discussion.)

1.2.1: Debate (*vāda*) is the undertaking of a thesis and its counter-thesis, employing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) for proof and refutation, not contradicting established tenets (*siddhānta*), and consisting of the five members [of a syllogism]. 1.2.2: Sophistry (*jalpa*) is the employment of means of proof and refutation through quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), while conforming to the aforementioned [requirements of debate].
1.2.3: That same [kind of] debate (jalpa), when devoid of the establishment of a counter-position, is cavil (vitaṇḍā).
[This is the definition of cavil.]

[The Section on Fallacious Reasons] 1.2.4: The fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are the inconclusive (savyabhicāra), the contradictory (viruddha), the equal to the point at issue (prakaraṇasama), the equal to the probandum (sādhyasama), and the mistimed (kālātīta). [This is the aphorism enumerating the fallacious reasons.]
1.2.5: The inconclusive [reason] is that which deviates;
[the definition of deviation]. 1.2.6: That which contradicts a tenet after having accepted it is the contradictory [reason].
1.2.7: *Viruddha-lakṣaṇam* (The definition of the contradictory):
That from which there arises an inquiry regarding the subject under discussion, and which is adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion, is the *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced).
This is the definition of *prakaraṇasama*.
1.2.8: That which is not distinct from the probandum (sādhya) because it is itself yet to be proven is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama). [This is the definition of sādhyasama.
1.2.9: That which is stated when the proper time has passed is "mistimed" (kālātīta).
The definition of *kālātīta* (missing the proper time):
[The section on *chala* (quibble)] 1.2.10: *Chala* is the refutation of a statement by means of an alternative interpretation of its meaning.

The definition of quibble (chala) [NS 1.2.11]: It is of three kinds—quibble regarding speech (vākchala), quibble regarding a general term (sāmānyacchala), and quibble regarding metaphorical usage (upacāracchala).
This is the aphorism enumerating the divisions of quibble.

1.2.12: *Vākchala* (quibble with respect to speech) is the imagining of a different meaning from what was intended by the speaker, when the meaning expressed is non-specific. 1.2.13: *Sāmānyacchala* (quibble with respect to a genus) is the imagining of an impossible meaning due to the application of a too-general term to a possible meaning.

1.2.14: The definition of *sāmānyacchala* (quibble on the general): The denial of the actual existence of a thing when its description is based on a distinction of properties. The definition of *upacāracchala* (quibble on metaphorical usage).

1.2.15: Sophistry based on figurative usage (*upacāracchala*) is merely sophistry based on verbal expression (*vākchala*), because there is no distinction [between them]. [This is the definition of the prima facie argument for sophistry based on figurative usage. 1.2.16: It is not so, because it is a different thing [from verbal sophistry].
The definition of quibble regarding metaphorical usage (upacāracchala):
1.2.17: Otherwise, if [all cases] were treated as indistinguishable due to some commonality, it would follow that there is only one kind of quibble.
This is the definition of quibble regarding metaphorical usage.

[The General Section on Fallacies of the Probans] 1.2.18: A *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is an opposition based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). This is the definition of a *jāti*.

1.2.19: Misapprehension and non-apprehension are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). 1.2.20: From their various subdivisions, there arises a multiplicity of futile rejoinders (*jāti*) and points of defeat.
{The Sūtra on the Multiplicity of Points of Defeat} (Thus ends the second daily lesson of the first chapter in the Nyāyasūtra;
and this first chapter is completed.)
(Now the second chapter) (The first daily lesson) [The Section on the Examination of Doubt]

2.1.1: Doubt does not arise from the determination of common or multiple properties, nor from the determination of one or another property. 2.1.2: Nor does it arise from the determination of conflicting opinions or lack of stability.
{Doubt}: 2.1.3: And doubt arises from conflicting opinions regarding what is actually established.
2.1.4: [Doubt arises] because uncertainty is not fixed in itself, since uncertainty is not established as a fixed state.
2.1.5: Likewise, there would be perpetual doubt, because the continuous presence of those [doubtful] attributes is possible.
{Doubt}:
2.1.6: From the aforementioned determination itself, when there is a dependence on its specific qualities, doubt arises; it is neither a state of no doubt nor an absolute doubt.
{Doubt}

2.1.7: Where there is doubt, there follows this successive application [of the method of inquiry]; [this concludes the section on the examination of the general nature of the means of valid cognition].
2.1.8: Perception and the other means of knowledge are not valid, because they cannot be established in any of the three periods of time.
{This is the sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).} 2.1.9:
For if the means of knowledge must first be established, perception cannot arise from the contact of the sense organs with their objects.
{Pūrvapakṣasūtra} 2.1.10: If [the means of knowledge] are established subsequently, there is no establishment of the objects of knowledge from the means of knowledge.
{Pūrvapakṣasūtra}

2.1.11: If [cognitions] were established simultaneously, there would be an absence of sequential occurrence because each cognition is restricted to its own respective object. {This is the sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).} 2.1.12: Since [the existence of cognitions] cannot be established across the three periods of time, the prohibition [of their simultaneity] is untenable.
{Pūrvapakṣasūtra} 2.1.13: Furthermore, because all means of valid cognition are negated, the negation itself is untenable.
{Pūrvapakṣasūtra}

2.1.14: Or, if that [scripture] is authoritative, there is no sublation of all means of valid cognition. {This is a sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).} 2.1.15: And there is no sublation [of the scripture] with respect to the three times, because of the word [itself], just as the existence of a drum is established by its sound. Its establishment [is thus possible].
{Thesis Sūtra} 2.1.16: And [the means of knowledge] is itself an object of knowledge, like the validity of a scale. {Thesis Sūtra}
2.1.17: Since [the existence of] means of valid cognition is established by means of valid cognition, it follows that there must be an infinite regress of further means of valid cognition.
{This is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣasūtra).} 2.1.18:
Or, because of the cessation of that [infinite regress], just as the means of valid cognition are established, so too are the objects of valid cognition established.
{Thesis Sūtra} 2.1.19: No, because its establishment is like the establishment of the light of a lamp. {Definition of the Established Conclusion}
2.1.20: Because cessation is observed in some cases and non-cessation is observed in others, there is uncertainty regarding the definition of a tenet (*siddhāntalakṣaṇa*).
[From the Section on the Examination of Direct Perception (*pratyakṣaparīkṣāprakaraṇa*)].
2.1.21: The definition of perception is untenable because it is incomplete;
[this is] the examination of the definition of perception.
2.1.22: There is no production of perception in the absence of contact between the self and the mind.
2.1.23: By this same [reasoning], there would be an over-extension to direction, space, time, and ether as well.
2.1.24: Since the self has cognition as its inferential mark, it is not excluded [from being an object of inference].

{The aphorism on the definition of perception as a tenet} 2.1.25: And because it is characterized by the non-simultaneity [of cognitions], the mind is not [perceptible]. {The aphorism on the definition of perception as a tenet}
2.1.26: And because contact between the sense organ and its object is the cause of perception, it is stated by its own name [in the definition of perception].

(Sūtra on the established tenet of the definition of perception) 2.1.27: And because for those who are asleep or whose minds are distracted, [perception] has as its cause the contact between the sense organ and its object.
{Pratyakṣalakṣaṇa-siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.28: And by these [characteristics], there is the designation of specific types of cognition.
{Pratyakṣalakṣaṇa-siddhānta-sūtra}
2.1.29: It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory.
{Pratyakṣalakṣaṇa-siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.30: No, because of the predominance of a specific object.
{Pratyakṣalakṣaṇa-siddhānta-sūtra} [Chapter on the Examination of Objects] 2.1.31: Perception is inference because it is an apprehension resulting from the grasping of a single part.
{Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra} 2.1.32: No, because even that which is limited [in scope] is apprehended by perception.
{Siddhānta-sūtra}

2.1.33: Nor is there perception of only one part [of an object], because of the existence of the whole. [This is a sūtra of established tenet; it introduces an examination of the whole as a corollary.]
2.1.34: There is doubt regarding the whole because it is yet to be proven. {Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra} 2.1.35: There would be no perception of anything at all if the whole were not established.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.36: And because holding and drawing [objects] are possible.
{Siddhānta-sūtra}
2.1.37: If it is argued that the perception [of atoms] is like that of an army or a forest, we say no, because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses.
[Siddhānta-sūtra] (Examination of Inference).
2.1.38: Inference is not a valid means of knowledge because of deviation [from the rule] due to obstruction, injury, and similarity.
{Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra} 2.1.39: No, because [in those cases] there is a different object [of inference] due to partial fear and similarity.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} {Examination of the Present Time} 2.1.40: The non-existence of the present.
[Objection Sūtra 2.1.41]: Because of the impossibility of the time for falling and that which has fallen or is about to fall,
there is likewise the non-existence of those two if the present does not exist.
Because of that dependence,
[Siddhānta-sūtra 2.1.42 states]: "There is no establishment of the past and the future through mutual dependence."
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.43: In the absence of the present, there would be no apprehension of anything at all, because perception would be impossible.
{Siddhānta-sūtra}
2.1.44: However, because both the state of being already accomplished and the state of being yet to be accomplished are possible, there is an apprehension in both ways.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} [The Section on the Examination of Analogy]
2.1.45: The definition of comparison (*upamāna*) is not established because of similarity that is absolute, predominant, or partial.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.46: Since comparison is established through well-known similarity, the aforementioned defects do not apply.
{Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra} 2.1.47: Because that which is not perceived is established by means of perception.
{Siddhānta-sūtra}
2.1.48: We do not see the purpose of comparison (*upamāna*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when the gavaya is not perceived.
(Siddhānta-sūtra) 2.1.49: Because comparison is established through the application [of the word] "so" (*tathā*), there is no lack of distinction.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} [The Section on the Examination of the Generality of Sound] 2.1.50: Sound is inference, because the object [denoted by it] is not perceived [directly] and is therefore inferable.
{Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra} 2.1.51: Because perception does not function in two ways.
{Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra}
2.1.52: And because of the [established] relationship.
2.1.53: From a word, there arises a comprehension of the object through the power of the instruction of a reliable person.
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 2.1.54: And because filling, burning, and splitting are not perceived, there is an absence of connection.
*Siddhānta-sūtra*.
2.1.55: There is no refutation [of the self] because of the established relation between word and meaning.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.56: No, because the comprehension of the meaning of a word is based on convention.
And because there is no fixed rule regarding specific classes [of words], [the suffix is applied];
this is a siddhānta-sūtra. (2.1.57)
[The Section Examining Specific Verbal Testimony] 2.1.58: Its lack of authority [is established] due to the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology.
(Siddhānta-sūtra)
2.1.59: No, because of the deficiency in the object, the agent, and the instrument.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.60: Because, having admitted [the opponent's position], a fault is stated regarding the difference in time.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.61: And because the justification for restatement is established.
{Siddhānta-sūtra}
2.1.62: And because the division of sentences is established by the inclusion of the meaning [of the words].
2.1.63: Because of the application of speech as injunction (*vidhi*), explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and restatement (*anuvāda*).
Siddhānta-sūtra 2.1.64: An injunction (vidhi) is that which prescribes (vidhāyaka).
2.1.65: Praise, censure, the deeds of others, and ancient history constitute *arthavāda* (explanatory passage).
[This is a *siddhānta-sūtra*;
it is a classification of *arthavāda*.]
2.1.66: An *anuvāda* is the restatement of that which has been prescribed by an injunction (*vidhi*).
2.1.67: There is no distinction between an *anuvāda* and a *punarukta* (repetition).
Because the practice of words is possible (Śabdābhyāsopapattiḥ),
Sūtra 2.1.68: as in the instruction for moving more quickly, there is no lack of distinction due to practice.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.1.69: And its authority is like the authority of the Mantras and Āyurveda,
because of the authority of the trustworthy person.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} (Thus ends the first Āhnika of the second Adhyāya in the Nyāyasūtra) (The second Āhnika)
[The Examination of the Fourfold Nature of the Means of Valid Cognition] 2.2.1: There are not four [means of valid cognition],
because tradition (aitihya), presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), probability (sambhava), and non-existence (abhāva) are also means of valid cognition.

{Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra} 2.2.2: There is no refutation [of the definition of verbal testimony], because tradition (aitihya) is not distinct from verbal testimony, and because presumption (arthāpatti), probability (sambhava), and absence (abhāva) are not distinct from inference.
{Siddhānta-sūtra}
2.2.3: Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not a valid means of knowledge because it is inconclusive.
{Examination of the Validity of Presumption} 2.2.4: Because there is a misconception of presumption where there is no presumption.
2.2.5: "The non-conclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). 2.2.6: "And the invalidity of the negation [of that] is due to its being non-conclusive;
or, if that [negation] were valid, there would be no invalidity of presumptive testimony."

{Siddhānta-sūtra} [Establishment of Non-existence as a Means of Valid Cognition – Sub-section] 2.2.7: There is no validity to non-existence as a means of cognition, because its object of cognition is not established.

{Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra} 2.2.8: Because that which is not characterized is established as an object of knowledge through the fact that it is characterized by the absence of characteristics in those things that have been characterized. {Example-sūtra}
2.2.9: If it is argued that there is no non-existence when an object is absent, we say no, because another definition [of non-existence] is applicable.
(Siddhānta-sūtra)
2.2.10: That [reason] is not a valid reason (ahetu) with respect to things that are uncharacterized;
[this is the *pūrvapakṣa-sūtra*].
2.2.11: No, because [the reason] is established in dependence on those things that abide according to their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 2.2.12: Because non-existence prior to origination is logically established.
*Siddhānta-sūtra*.
2.2.13: [Sound is non-eternal] because it has a beginning, because it is perceptible by the senses, and because it is treated as something produced.
2.2.14: No, because the universal of the absence of a jar is eternal, and because even in the case of eternal things, there is a figurative treatment as if they were non-eternal.
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 2.2.15:
There is no deviation [from the rule] because of the distinction between the primary sense and its figurative application;
[this is a sūtra establishing the non-eternality of sound].
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.2.16: Because of the qualification by the inference of a continuum,
{the sūtra establishing the non-eternality of sound}.
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 2.2.17: Because the substance that is the cause [of sound] is denoted by the term "part" (*pradeśa*),
this is the sūtra establishing the non-eternality of sound.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.2.18: Because [sound] is not perceived prior to its utterance, and because no obstruction or other cause for non-perception is perceived,
[this is a sūtra establishing the non-eternality of sound].
2.2.19: Because that [obstruction] is not perceived, its existence is established due to its non-perception; [this is the sūtra for establishing the non-eternality of sound].
2.2.20: Because there is no non-perception—due to the actual existence of the non-perception itself—there is no impossibility of an obstruction, since it is not perceived.
Siddhānta-sūtra 2.2.21: Because non-apprehension consists in the nature of non-perception, it is not a valid reason.
Siddhānta-sūtra.
2.2.22: Because it is intangible.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.2.23: No, because action is non-eternal.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.2.24: No, because the atom is eternal.
{Siddhānta-sūtra}
2.2.25: [This follows] from the recipient (sampradāna). 2.2.26: Because that which lies between them is not perceived, it is not a valid reason (ahetu).
Siddhānta-sūtra 2.2.27: There is no prohibition [of the Veda] because of its being taught.
Siddhānta-sūtra.
2.2.28: There is no prohibition [of the self as the agent of knowledge] because it is taught as one of the two sides;
[this is a *siddhānta-sūtra*].
2.2.29: Because of repetition.
Siddhānta-sūtra 2.2.30: Even when there is difference, [the term "repetition" applies] because of figurative usage.
Siddhānta-sūtra.
2.2.31: "Because one thing is not non-different from another, it is not non-different; thus, there is an absence of otherness.
[Siddhānta-sūtra] 2.2.32: "In the absence of that, there is no non-otherness."
Because the establishment of those two is mutually dependent (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.33):
because no cause of destruction is perceived.
Siddhānta-sūtra 2.2.34: Since no cause for non-hearing is perceived, there would be the undesirable consequence of constant hearing.
2.2.35: Since non-apprehension does not exist when that which is apprehensible is present, it is not a valid reason (*anapadeśa*).
(Siddhānta-sūtra) 2.2.36: Due to the conjunction with the cause of the hand, there is no non-apprehension [of sound] when the sound has ceased.
Siddhānta Sūtra 2.2.37: And because no cause of destruction is perceived, there follows the undesirable consequence that [the object] is eternal if it persists.
2.2.38: There is no prohibition [of the suffix -matup] because of the lack of tangibility.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 2.2.39: And because another case-ending is applicable in a compound.
Siddhānta-sūtra 2.2.40: There is doubt because of the teaching of both modification and substitution.
[Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra]

5.1.1: The similar (*sādharmya*), dissimilar (*vaidharmya*), equalizing by superiority (*utkarṣa*), equalizing by inferiority (*apakarṣa*), equalizing the praiseworthy (*varṇya*), equalizing the unpraiseworthy (*avarṇya*), equalizing by alternative (*vikalpa*), equalizing by attainment (*sādhyaprāpti*), equalizing by non-attainment (*aprāpti*), equalizing by consequence (*prasaṅga*), equalizing by counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), equalizing by non-arising (*anutpatti*), equalizing by doubt (*saṃśaya*), equalizing by the topic (*prakaraṇa*), equalizing by the reason (*hetu*), equalizing by implication (*arthāpatti*), equalizing by non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), equalizing by proof (*upapatti*), equalizing by perception (*upalabdhi*), equalizing by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), and equalizing by the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānitya*) are [the fallacies of] equalization (*jāti*).
[Siddhānta-sūtra]

5.1.2: When a conclusion is drawn through similarity or dissimilarity, the [objections] known as *sādharmya-sama* (balancing the similarity) and *vaidharmya-sama* (balancing the dissimilarity) arise because the opposite of that property is established.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.3: Its establishment is like the establishment of "cowness" from a cow; [therefore, the objection is invalid].

*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.4: Because of the variation in properties of the probandum and the example, and because both are to be proven, there are [the fallacies of] *utkarṣasama*, *apakarṣasama*, *varṇyasama*, *vikalpasama*, and *sādhyasama*.
5.1.5: There is no refutation on the basis of dissimilarity, because the conclusion is established through some degree of similarity.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.6: And because the example is applicable due to the extension of the property to be proven.

*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.7: Because a reason is indistinguishable whether it reaches the probandum or does not reach it— since it cannot establish [the probandum] by reaching it, nor can it establish it by not reaching it— the two [objections] are "balancing the reached" (*prāptisama*) and "balancing the unreached" (*aprāptisama*).

5.1.8: There is no prohibition [against the production of sound] because we observe the production of jars and other objects, and because [sound] is produced by pressure, as in the case of sorcery (*abhicāra*).

{Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.9: The two fallacies *prasaṅgasama* (balancing the consequence) and *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* (balancing the counter-example) consist in opposing [the argument] by pointing out that the reason for the example has not been stated, and by adducing a counter-example.
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.10: Its cessation is like the cessation of the application of the material cause of a lamp.
*Siddhānta-sūtra*.
5.1.11: And when there is the status of a counter-example and a reason, the example is not a non-reason.
(Siddhānta-sūtra) 5.1.12: The "balancing the non-arising" (anutpattisama) [fallacy] occurs because of the absence of a cause prior to arising.
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.13: Because that which has arisen exists in such a manner, and because a cause is logically established, there is no negation of the cause.
*Siddhānta-sūtra*.

5.1.14: Since the general property (*sāmānya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are equally perceptible by the senses, the "balancing of doubt" (*saṃśayasama*) occurs because of the commonality of both permanence and impermanence.

(Siddhānta-sūtra) 5.1.15: When there is doubt based on similarity, there should not be doubt based on dissimilarity; otherwise, if doubt were to arise from both, it would lead to the consequence of perpetual doubt. Furthermore, since the existence of the general property is not denied, [the objection] is not a valid refutation.
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.16: *Prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced reason) occurs because the establishment of the process [of proof] results from the similarity of both [reasons].
5.1.17: Since the subject matter is established by means of a counter-argument, the refutation [of that argument] is untenable, because the counter-argument is valid.
(Siddhānta-sūtra) 5.1.18: Because a reason cannot be established across the three periods of time, there is the "balancing of the non-reason" (*ahetusama*).
Siddhānta-sūtra 5.1.19: Since the probandum is not established by means of a reason, there is no establishment [of the reason] across the three times.

5.1.20: And because a negation is impossible, there is no negation of that which is to be negated. {Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.21: Arthāpattisama (the equal by implication) occurs when the opponent's position is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

*Siddhāntasūtra* 5.1.22: The argument that [the opponent's] position is undermined by implication because it was not explicitly stated is untenable, because that which was not stated is inconclusive and because implication itself is uncertain. *Siddhāntasūtra*.

5.1.23: "The equalization based on non-distinction due to the occurrence of existence" [is that objection which,] because a single property occurs [in all things], results in the consequence of non-distinction among all things; [this is a *siddhānta-sūtra*].
5.1.24: Because in some cases a property is impossible and in other cases it is possible, there is no [absolute] negation.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.25: The "balancing of the possible" (upapattisama) occurs because the reasons for both [the presence and absence of a property] are equally possible.
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.26: There is no prohibition [of the soul's activity] because of the non-apprehension of the causes for its production.
*Siddhānta-sūtra*.
5.1.27: [The fallacy of] "balancing the perception" (*upalabdhisama*) occurs because [the probandum] is perceived even in the absence of the stated cause.
5.1.28: There is no refutation [of the original position], because that property can also arise from another cause.

*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.29: When the non-existence [of something] is established because it is not perceived due to its non-perception, the *anupalabdhisama* (balancing the non-perception) occurs because the opposite of that [non-existence] is possible. *Siddhānta-sūtra*.
5.1.30: Non-apprehension is not a valid reason, because its nature is that of non-perception.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.31: And because one internally experiences the existence and non-existence of various cognitions.

*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.32: *Anityasama* (the fallacy of the "equal to the non-eternal") occurs because, due to similarity— that is, the occurrence of a common property— the consequence follows that everything must be non-eternal.

5.1.33: Because [the reason] is unestablished due to similarity, the refutation is unestablished; and because it shares the same properties as that which is to be refuted. 5.1.34: Furthermore, there is no lack of distinction [between the two cases], because the property known in the example through its relationship as the probandum and the probans exists in both ways [in the subject].

*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.35: *Nityasama* (the equalizing of the eternal) occurs when, because of the existence of the non-eternal within the eternal, one establishes the eternity [of the subject] on the grounds that it exists in the non-eternal. *Siddhānta-sūtra*.
5.1.36: There is no [valid] negation because the impermanent exists eternally within that which is to be negated; for impermanence is established in the impermanent.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.37: The "balancing the effect" (kāryasama) [fallacy occurs] because the effects of effort are manifold.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.38: When there is a difference in the effect, effort is not the cause, because the presence of causes for non-perception is established.
{Siddhānta-sūtra}
5.1.39: Even in the case of a prohibition, the same fault applies.
(Siddhānta-sūtra) 5.1.40: It is thus in all cases.
*Siddhānta-sūtra* 5.1.41: In the case of a counter-prohibition, the fault is the same as the fault in the original prohibition.

5.1.42: Having accepted a refutation as faulty, when there is a counter-refutation, the recurrence of the same fault constitutes *matānujñā* (concession of one's own position). {Siddhānta-sūtra} 5.1.43: When one presents a conclusion based on a reason that requires the definition of one’s own position and its supporting proof, the recurrence of the same fault occurs because one has accepted the faults of the opponent’s position.
{Siddhānta-sūtra} (Thus ends the first Āhnika of the fifth Adhyāya in the Nyāyasūtra) (The second Āhnika)

5.2.1: Abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), shifting the proposition (*pratijñāntara*), contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*), renunciation of the proposition (*pratijñāsannyāsa*), a different reason (*hetvantara*), an irrelevant matter (*arthāntara*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*), the incoherent (*apārthaka*), the mistimed (*aprāptakāla*), the deficient (*nyūna*), the redundant (*adhika*), the repetitive (*punarukta*), failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*),

lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), inability to respond (*apratibhā*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), admission of one's own position (*matānujñā*), neglecting to censure when it is censurable (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), and censuring what is not censurable (*niranuyojyānuyoga*).
Deviation from tenets and fallacious reasons are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

[Nigrahasthāna-uddeśa-sūtra 5.2.2: "The abandonment of one's own proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) occurs when one admits the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) into one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*)."

{The Sūtra on the Definition of Abandoning the Proposition} 5.2.3: When the object of the proposition has been refuted, the specification of another meaning by means of a conceptual differentiation of its properties is "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*). {The Sūtra on the Definition of Shifting the Proposition}
5.2.4: Contradiction between the proposition and the reason is "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*). [This is the definition-sūtra for contradiction of the proposition.
5.2.5: When the thesis is refuted, the withdrawal of the meaning of the proposition is "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāsannyāsa*).
5.2.6: *Pratijñāsannyāsa* (Abandonment of the Proposition).

5.2.7: *Hetvantara* (Quibble regarding the Reason): When a reason has been stated without qualification and is refuted, the proponent's desire for a qualification constitutes a different reason (*hetvantara*).

5.2.7: *Arthāntara* (Irrelevant) is that which has a meaning unrelated to the subject matter under discussion. 5.2.8: *Nirarthaka* (Meaningless) is like the mere enumeration of a sequence of phonemes.

{The definition-sūtra for the meaningless (nirarthaka):} 5.2.9: That which, even when stated three times by the proponent to the assembly and the opponent, is not understood is "the unintelligible" (*avijñātārtha*).
{The definition-sūtra for the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*):}

5.2.10: That which has a disconnected meaning due to the lack of proper sequence between preceding and succeeding parts is the "meaningless" (apārthaka). 5.2.11: A statement in which the members [of a syllogism] are inverted is "untimely" (aprāptakāla).
5.2.12: A statement whose timing is not appropriate is a *lakṣaṇa-sūtra*.
5.2.13: That which is deficient by even one of its constituent members is *nyūna* (deficient); this is the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* for *nyūna*.

5.2.13: That which has an excess of reason (*hetu*) or example (*udāharaṇa*) is "redundant" (*adhika*). 5.2.14: The restatement of words or their meanings is "tautology" (*punarukta*), except in the case of a restatement for the sake of corroboration (*anuvāda*).

The definition-sūtra [5.2.14] was restated as 5.2.15: "But in the case of a restatement (anuvāda), there is no tautology, because a repetition of words is justified by a specific difference in meaning.
[This is the sūtra that provides an exception to the definition of tautology.]
5.2.16: Repetition (*punarukta*) is the restatement, by its own word, of what has already been understood through the sense; [this is a rule that constitutes an exception to the definition].
5.2.17: Non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is the failure to restate what has been understood by the assembly, even though it has been stated three times.
5.2.18: *Ananubhāṣaṇam* (Failure to Reproduce) is a definition-sūtra;
5.2.19: *Avijñātam* (Not Understanding) and *Ajñānam* (Ignorance) are definition-sūtras.
5.2.19: Non-perception of the opponent's [argument] is "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*).
5.2.20: Interruption of the discussion due to attachment to other tasks is "distraction" (*vikṣepa*).
{Deflection (vikṣepa): Characteristic Sūtra} 5.2.21: Pointing out a fault in the opponent's position by admitting a fault in one's own position is "admission of an opinion" (matānujñā).
{Admission of an Opinion (matānujñā): Characteristic Sūtra}
5.2.22: Not pointing out a point of defeat when it has been reached is "overlooking the censurable" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*).
[This is the definition-sūtra for *paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*. 5.2.23: Charging with a point of defeat where there is no point of defeat is "reproaching the non-censurable" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*).

{The Sūtra on the Definition of Rebuttal of the Non-Reprovable} 5.2.24: Having accepted a tenet, engaging in a discussion without restriction [thereof] is *apasiddhānta* (the fallacy of deviating from a tenet). {The Sūtra on the Definition of *Apasiddhānta*}

5.2.25: And the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are as previously stated. (Thus ends the second daily lesson of the fifth chapter in the *Nyāyasūtra*: "The Examination of Fallacies of the Reason.")
(And this fifth chapter is completed) The Nyāya-darśana is finished.
